claim: Taenia solium is ranked as the foodborne parasitic infection contributing the highest number of disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs), an estimated 2.78 million DALYs in 2010.
source: Globally, T. solium is ranked as the foodborne parasitic infection contributing the highest number of disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs), an estimated 2.78 million DALYs in 2010 (Havelaar et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Havelaar et al., 2015, which provides the specific DALY estimate.

claim: Neurocysticercosis causes approximately one third of epilepsy/seizure disorders in endemic settings.
source: Neurocysticercosis is responsible for the major health burden associated with T. solium, causing approximately one third of epilepsy/seizure disorders in endemic settings (Gripper and Welburn, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gripper and Welburn, 2017.

claim: The WHO 2021–2030 NTD roadmap proposes that 30% of endemic countries achieve intensified T. solium control in hyperendemic areas by 2030.
source: The World Health Organization (WHO) 2021–2030 Neglected Tropical Diseases roadmap has proposed that 30% of endemic countries achieve intensified T. solium control in hyperendemic areas by 2030.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and references the WHO roadmap.

claim: Control strategies for T. solium have proven efficacious in field studies but no large-scale interventions have been rolled out as part of national NTD programmes.
source: These control strategies have proven efficacious in field studies (de Coster et al., 2018; Dixon et al., 2021), but to date no large-scale interventions have been rolled out as part of national Neglected Tropical Disease (NTD) programmes, and therefore their impact alone or in combination in different epidemiological settings remains poorly understood and/or modelled (CystiTeam Group for Epidemiology and Modelling of Taenia solium Taeniasis/Cysticercosis, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to field studies (de Coster et al., 2018; Dixon et al., 2021) and a modeling group report (CystiTeam Group, 2019).

claim: The WHO NTD 2021–2030 roadmap focuses on achieving intensified control in hyperendemic areas of 17 (27%) endemic countries.
source: The milestones proposed in the new World Health Organization (WHO) NTD 2021–2030 roadmap (Havelaar et al., 2015; World Health Organization, 2020) focus on achieving intensified control in hyperendemic areas of 17 (27%) endemic countries.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the WHO roadmap documents (Havelaar et al., 2015; World Health Organization, 2020).

claim: Endemicity levels for T. solium have not been defined in terms of infection indicators.
source: However, endemicity levels for T. solium have not been defined in terms of infection indicators and there exist limited data on the geographical distribution of T. solium prevalence at national scales.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text as a knowledge gap.

claim: After systematic review screening, a total of 16 studies were included in the analysis, originating from South America (n=4), Africa (n=8) and Asia (n=4).
source: After title, abstract and full-text eligibility screening of 236 studies initially identified (01/11/2014 to 02/10/2019), and 11 studies included in the Coral-Almeida et al., 2015 literature review, a total of 16 studies were included in the analysis (PRISMA flowchart; Figure 1), originating from South America (n=4), Africa (n=8) and Asia (n=4) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and split by n=4 HTT and n=15 HCC surveys (full details in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the systematic review process described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1 (PRISMA flowchart).

claim: Total sample sizes were 6,653 individuals across HTT surveys with individual age range of <1–96 years.
source: Total sample sizes were 6,653 individuals (range 576–4599; with individual age range of <1–96 years) across HTT surveys, which included three copro-Ag-based surveys and one Ab-based survey
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific sample size data from the included studies.

claim: Observed seroprevalence ranged from 4.5% to 23.4% for HTT surveys.
source: Observed (sero)prevalence ranged from 4.5% to 23.4% (95% confidence interval (CI) range: 3.0–24.6%) for HTT surveys
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific prevalence ranges from the data.

claim: Hyperendemic transmission settings are defined as those with all-age observed HTT (sero)prevalence of ≥3% and all-age observed HCC (sero)prevalence of ≥6%.
source: We defined hyperendemic transmission settings as those with all-age observed HTT (sero)prevalence of ≥3% and all-age observed HCC (sero)prevalence of ≥6%. Studies with (sero)prevalence values below these were defined as endemic transmission settings. These putative endemicity definitions were defined following a literature review of studies referring to 'hyper' or 'highly' endemic settings (Supplementary file 2 with additional explanatory text in Appendix 1).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a definition developed by the authors based on a literature review.

claim: For the copro-Ag ELISA datasets, DIC scores were similar (within one unit) between models with and without infection loss.
source: For the copro-Ag ELISA datasets (to which models were jointly fitted to yield a single sensitivity and specificity posterior), DIC scores were similar (within one unit) between models with and without infection loss (Table 1 and Figure 3a), indicating limited information to differentiate between model fits.
evidence: The claim is supported by DIC scores presented in Table 1 and Figure 3a.

claim: The copro-Ag ELISA datasets were found in hyperendemic settings in Zambia (6.3%) and Brazil (4.5%).
source: The copro-Ag ELISA datasets (Gomes et al., 2002; Mwape et al., 2012) were found in hyperendemic settings (all-age HTT (sero)prevalence ≥3%) in Zambia (6.3%) (Mwape et al., 2012) and Brazil (4.5%) (Gomes et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific prevalence values and citations.

claim: HCC Ab-seroconversion with Ab-seroreversion (reversible model) provided an improved joint fit to the multiple datasets based on the LLGP-EITB assay.
source: HCC Ab-seroconversion with Ab-seroreversion (reversible model) provided an improved joint fit to the multiple datasets based on the antibody lentil lectin-purified glycoprotein enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot (LLGP-EITB) assay (Tsang et al., 1989; Table 2 and Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by model comparison results presented in Table 2 and Figure 4a.

claim: HCC infection acquisition with infection loss (reversible model) provided an improved fit for models fitted jointly to multiple datasets based on B158/B60 Ag-ELISA.
source: HCC infection acquisition with infection loss (reversible model) provided an improved fit for models fitted jointly to multiple datasets based on B158/B60 Ag-ELISA (Brandt et al., 1992; Dorny et al., 2000; Table 3 and Figure 5a)
evidence: The claim is supported by model comparison results presented in Table 3 and Figure 5a.

claim: HCC Ab-seroconversion with Ab-seroreversion (reversible model) provided an improved fit across 23 departments of Colombia.
source: HCC Ab-seroconversion with Ab-seroreversion (reversible model), fitted to multiple datasets using an IgG Ab-ELISA (López et al., 1988), provided an improved fit across the 23 (out of a total of 24) departments of Colombia (Flórez Sánchez et al., 2013) included in the analysis.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with citation to the diagnostic method and data source.

claim: One department (Bolívar) was omitted from the Colombia analysis due to difficulty fitting to such a distinct age-seroprevalence profile.
source: One department (Bolívar) was omitted due to difficultly fitting to such a distinct age-seroprevalence profile (prevalence peak in early ages).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a methodological decision.

claim: There was substantial geographical variation in HCC FoI, Ab-seroreversion rate, and all-age seroprevalence across the 23 departments of Colombia.
source: Figure 7 highlights the geographical variation in a HCC Ab-seroconversion or FoI, (b) HCC Ab-seroreversion rate and c the HCC antibody all-age seroprevalence, across the 23 departments.
evidence: The claim is supported by the geographical variation shown in Figure 7.

claim: There was an overall decline in the average time until humans become HCC Ab-seropositive or infected with increasing all-age HCC (sero)prevalence.
source: Figure 8 shows an overall decline in the average time (in years) until humans become HCC Ab-seropositive or infected with increasing all-age HCC (sero)prevalence, noting 18 studies identified in endemic settings (0.48–5.71% all-age HCC (sero)prevalence), and 19 estimates in hyperendemic settings (6.33–38.68% all-age HCC seroprevalence).
evidence: The claim is supported by the trend shown in Figure 8.

claim: There was strong evidence for similar average durations of remaining Ab-seropositive across different endemicity settings and countries.
source: Figure 8b presents strong evidence for similar average durations of remaining Ab-seropositive (1/ρsero) across different endemicity settings and countries (Figure 8—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 8b.

claim: There was evidence for a trend of decreasing duration of humans remaining infected with increasing all-age prevalence in antigen-based studies.
source: However, there was evidence for a trend of decreasing duration of humans remaining infected (1/ρinf) with increasing all-age prevalence (antigen-based studies; n=5).
evidence: The claim is directly stated based on analysis of antigen-based studies.

claim: HTT FoI estimates ranged from 0.44 per 1,000 people per year for an endemic setting to 9.6-21 per 1000 per year for two hyperendemic settings.
source: We have also placed our HTT FoI estimates in the context of (putative) endemic or hyperendemic settings, with 0.44 per 1,000 people per year for a (single) endemic setting, and from 9.6 to 21 per 1000 per year for two hyperendemic settings.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific FoI estimates.

claim: HCC FoI estimates ranged from 0.086 to 21 per 1000 per year in endemic settings.
source: HCC FoI estimates ranged from 0.086 to 21 per 1000 per year in (18, including Colombian departments) endemic settings (0.086–21 for Ab-based surveys; 0.17–4.4 for Ag-based surveys)
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific FoI ranges.

claim: HCC FoI estimates ranged from 0.54 to 120 per 1000 per year in hyperendemic settings.
source: and from 0.54 to 120 per 1000 per year in (19) hyperendemic settings (2.3–120 for Ab-based surveys; 0.54–110 for Ag-based surveys).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific FoI ranges.

claim: Infection loss with infection acquisition was indicated for two HTT copro-Ag-ELISA-based surveys and five of six HCC antigen-based surveys.
source: Infection loss with infection acquisition was indicated for two HTT copro-Ag-ELISA-based surveys, and five of six HCC antigen-based surveys, supporting inclusion of parameters representing recovery from HTT and HCC in T. solium transmission models (Dixon et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated based on model fitting results.

claim: The duration of adult tapeworm infection ranges from 1.3 to 1.4 years with uncertainty bounds from 1.0 to 2.8 years.
source: Our infection loss rates for HTT indicate that the duration of adult tapeworm infection (the reciprocal of ρinf) ranges from 1.3 to 1.4 years (with uncertainty bounds from 1.0 to 2.8 years), aligning with literature estimates suggesting that adult tapeworms live for less than 5 years (Garcia et al., 2014), although our values are only based on two studies.
evidence: The claim is based on calculated reciprocals of infection loss rates from the study data, with comparison to literature estimates.

claim: HCC Ab-seroreversion rates are consistently larger than HCC Ab-seroconversion rates across settings.
source: HCC Ab-seroreversion rates (or infection loss rates) from this analysis are also consistently larger than HCC Ab-seroconversion rates (or infection acquisition rates), in agreement with comparisons of HCC Ab-seroreversion to Ab-seroconversion (or Ag-seroreversion to Ag-seroconversion) estimates in the literature, which are generally based on cumulative seroconversion and seroreversion proportions, or rule-based modelling approaches (Dermauw et al., 2018; Garcia et al., 2001; Coral-Almeida et al., 2015; Mwape et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's data analysis and comparison with literature estimates.

claim: High cysticercosis Ab-seroreversion rates are likely indicative of substantial transient responses generated from exposure without establishment of infection.
source: The high cysticercosis Ab-seroreversion rates indicated across datasets are likely indicative of substantial transient responses generated from exposure without establishment of infection.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the observed high seroreversion rates.

claim: There is no relationship between all-age Ab-seroprevalence and the average duration humans remain Ab-seropositive.
source: Since Ab-seroreversion or infection loss parameters were allowed to vary among settings, the consistency of the posterior estimates for these parameters indicates that rates of HCC Ab-seroreversion are stable (i.e. no relationship between all-age Ab-seroprevalence and the average duration humans remain Ab-seropositive, Figure 8b; no relationship between the Ab-seroconversion and Ab-seroreversion rates, Figure 8—figure supplement 2), confirming this a priori expectation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis results shown in Figure 8b.

claim: The average duration humans remain infected decreases with increasing seroprevalence in antigen-based studies.
source: The average duration humans remain infected (i.e., the reciprocal of the HCC infection loss rate), however, decreases with increasing seroprevalence (and a positive relationship between infection acquisition rates and infection loss rates, Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis results shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is substantial subnational variation in HCC FoI and Ab-seroreversion rates in Colombia.
source: Our results identify substantial subnational variation in HCC FoI (measured by Ab-seroconversion) and Ab-seroreversion rates.
evidence: The claim is directly stated based on the Colombia analysis results.

claim: There is only a limited relationship between HCC epidemiological quantities, Ab-seroprevalence and risk factors at the department level in Colombia.
source: There appears to be only a limited relationship between these epidemiological quantities, Ab-seroprevalence and other risk factors, including open defecation and pig ownership at the department level, highlighting the complex nature of exposure drivers for HCC.
evidence: The claim is directly stated based on the Colombia analysis.

claim: The southeastern rural departments of Vaupés and Amazonas in Colombia show the highest all-age seroprevalence and FoI estimates.
source: For example, the southeastern rural departments of Vaupés and Amazonas show the highest all-age seroprevalence and FoI estimates.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an example from the Colombia analysis.

claim: Spatial correlation in seropositivity was estimated up to approximately 140 km at the Municipality level in Colombia.
source: Spatial variation has been explored formally for this dataset by including spatial structure (i.e. spatial correlation in seropositivity estimated up to approximately 140 km at the Municipality level) into a risk factor analysis, and identifying hot spots of unexplained residual clustering in northern and southern municipalities in Colombia (Galipó et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Galipó et al., 2021.

claim: The copro-Ag ELISA for detecting adult tapeworm infection is not species specific.
source: For example, the widely used copro-Ag ELISA for detecting adult tapeworm infection is not species specific (Ng-Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ng-Nguyen et al., 2017.

claim: A proportion of positive results by both HCC Ag- and Ab- diagnostics may be due to transient responses and cross-reactions following exposure to eggs of other helminths.
source: Literature estimates indicate high specificity of HCC diagnostics; however, a proportion of positive results by both HCC Ag- and Ab- diagnostics may be due to transient responses and cross-reactions following exposure to the eggs of other other helminths including Taenia saginata, Echinoccous granulosus and Schistosomia species (Lightowlers et al., 2016b; Noh et al., 2014; Kojic and White, 2003; Furrows et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to literature on diagnostic cross-reactivity.

claim: The prevailing assumption governing the catalytic models is of a constant FoI with respect to age.
source: The prevailing (and most parsimonious) assumption governing the behaviour of the catalytic models fitted in this analysis is of a constant FoI with respect to age.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a methodological assumption.

claim: HTT copro-Ag-ELISA age-prevalence peaks in children have been observed in Peru, Guatemala and Zambia.
source: The observations of HTT copro-Ag-ELISA age-prevalence peaks/odds of infection in children from Peru, Guatemala and Zambia (Falcon et al., 2003; Allan et al., 1996; Mwape et al., 2015) suggest that these trends might be more widespread.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies in Peru, Guatemala and Zambia.

claim: Age peaks in HTT prevalence could indicate the need for targeted mass drug administration programmes to school-age children.
source: Age peaks in HTT prevalence could indicate the need for targeted mass drug administration (MDA) programmes, such as delivery of anthelminthics (praziquantel) to school-age children, an approach that could be integrated into existing schistosomiasis control programmes where HTT and schistosomiasis are co-endemic.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference about potential intervention strategies based on observed age patterns.

claim: There is marked geographical heterogeneity in FoI and associated all-age (sero)prevalence estimates for HCC.
source: The results presented here, particularly for HCC, where many datasets were available, suggest marked geographical heterogeneity in FoI and associated all-age (sero)prevalence estimates.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a summary of the results.

claim: There is strong evidence for both HCC Ab-seroreversion and infection loss.
source: There is strong evidence for both HCC Ab-seroreversion and infection loss, likely due to transient dynamics which highlights the need for careful interpretation of cross-sectional (sero)prevalence survey estimates.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a summary of the modeling results.

claim: Catalytic models provide useful tools for interpreting cross-sectional seroprevalence data.
source: Catalytic models provide useful tools for interpreting such data, which are far more abundant than a few longitudinal surveys reported in the literature.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a conclusion about the utility of the modeling approach.

claim: There is substantial subnational variation in exposure to HCC in Colombia.
source: We also quantify, for the first time, the presence of substantial subnational variation in exposure to HCC, highlighting the need for tailored, sub-national control strategies.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a key finding from the Colombia analysis.

claim: Flórez Sánchez et al., 2013 conducted a country-level survey of HCC antibody seroprevalence across 24 of Colombia's 32 administrative departments, sampling 29,360 individuals.
source: Flórez Sánchez et al., 2013 conducted a country-level survey of HCC antibody seroprevalence across 24 of Colombia's 32 administrative departments, sampling 29,360 individuals.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with citation to the data source.

claim: Age-seroprevalence profiles stratified by sex in each department of Colombia revealed no clear differences.
source: Age-seroprevalence profiles stratified by sex in each department revealed no clear differences (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), therefore age-seroprevalence data were not stratified by sex for further analysis (but see Galipó et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Simple and reversible catalytic models were originally proposed for fitting to epidemiological data by Muench, 1934.
source: Simple and reversible catalytic models (Figure 2), originally proposed for fitting to epidemiological data by Muench, 1934, were fitted to HTT and HCC age-(sero)prevalence profiles.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Muench, 1934.

claim: A weakly informative prior for λ was used for reversible model fits to prevent λ chains drifting to flat posterior space and failing to converge.
source: A weakly informative prior for λ, assuming a lognormal distribution (mean informed by the median estimate from the simple model fit, and a standard deviation of 1), was used for reversible model fits to prevent λ chains drifting to flat posterior space and failing to converge.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a methodological decision.

claim: The deviance information criterion (DIC) was used to compare individually- and jointly-fitted catalytic models.
source: The deviance information criterion (DIC) (Spiegelhalter et al., 2002) was used to compare individually- and jointly-fitted catalytic models.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with citation to the DIC method.

claim: Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo Metropolis–Hastings sampling algorithm was implemented to estimate the parameter posterior distribution.
source: A Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) Metropolis–Hastings sampling algorithm was implemented to estimate the parameter posterior distribution f(θ|r, n), assuming uniform prior distributions for λ and ρ (Table 4).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as the statistical method used.

claim: A maximum of 20,000,000 iterations were run for models fitted simultaneously to multiple datasets.
source: A maximum of 20,000,000 iterations were run for models fitted simultaneously to multiple datasets (2,000,000 for models fitted to single datasets) to obtain a sufficient sample to reduce autocorrelation through substantial subsampling, with the first 25% of runs being discarded as burn-in.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a methodological detail.

claim: The Madinga et al., 2017 dataset in the DRC was omitted from the models jointly fitted across copro-Ag ELISA datasets due to difficulty fitting catalytic models to such a distinct age-prevalence profile with a marked peak in early ages.
source: The Madinga et al., 2017 dataset in the DRC was omitted from the models jointly fitted across copro-Ag ELISA datasets, due to difficulty fitting catalytic models to such a distinct age-prevalence profile with a marked peak in early ages (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a methodological decision.

claim: The FoI for the best-fit model to the rES33-immunoblot antibody dataset in Lao PDR suggested a very low HTT Ab-seroconversion rate of 0.00046 year–1.
source: The FoI (λsero) for the best-fit model to the rES33-immunoblot antibody dataset in Lao PDR (Holt et al., 2016), suggested a very low HTT Ab-seroconversion rate of 0.00046 year–1
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific rate estimate from the model fitting.

claim: For models independently fitted to the single dataset from a hyperendemic setting in Kenya using the HP10 Ag-ELISA, the simple model without infection loss provided an improved fit.
source: For models fitted to the single dataset from a hyperendemic setting in Kenya (6.61%) (Wardrop et al., 2015), using the HP10 Ag-ELISA (Harrison et al., 1989), the (simple) model without infection loss provided an improved fit (Table 3 and Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by model comparison results in Table 3 and Figure 5b.
